description: Fox designs a toy playground: 18 fence pieces fit round it but 18 grass mats don't cover it. Area covers with unit squares, perimeter walks the edge, and Sheep's 12 fence pieces make pens with areas 5, 8 and 9 square metres.

youtube.title: Area and Perimeter Playground! Area and Perimeter for Kids | Grade 3 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Robo ordered 18 fence pieces and 18 grass mats for Fox's new playground. The fence fits perfectly, but the mats leave two bare squares. Why? Kids learn that area is how many unit squares cover a shape (square metres) and perimeter is the distance all the way round its edge (metres).

We name quadrilaterals by their sides and corners (rectangle, rhombus, square), cover a 4 by 5 play area with unit squares (4 x 5 = 20 square metres), walk its edge (4 + 5 + 4 + 5 = 18 metres), fix Robo's border-square mix-up, and help Sheep find the grassiest pen: with the same 12 fence pieces, pens of 1 by 5, 2 by 4 and 3 by 3 hold 5, 8 and 9 square metres. Then: area or perimeter for real jobs, a missing side, and a quiz.

For third graders (CCSS 3.G.A.1, 3.MD.C.5, 3.MD.C.6, 3.MD.C.7, 3.MD.D.8).

Try at home: cover a book with sticky notes in rows and count them (area), then wrap a string round it and measure the string (perimeter). Draw every rectangle with a perimeter of 12 squares on graph paper: which holds the most? Use scissors with a grown-up.

do.text: Area and Perimeter Playground
Look, Robo! My plan for a new toy playground.
The play area is four metres by five metres.
I ordered eighteen fence pieces, one metre each. And eighteen grass mats.
Same number. Done!
18 fence pieces
The fence fits all the way round. Perfect!
Will eighteen mats cover the play area? What do you think?
18 grass mats
Oh no! Two bare squares in the corner.
Same number, but one fit and one didn't. Why? Let's build it and see!
First, playground shapes. Each of these has four sides.
Any shape with four straight sides is a quadrilateral.
quadrilateral = 4 sides
This is my corner tester. It checks for a square corner, also called a right angle.
square corner = right angle
The rectangle: every corner fits the tester. Four square corners.
The square fits the tester too. And all four sides are the same length.
What about this slanted one?
No square corners. But its four sides are all equal. It's a rhombus.
This one has no equal sides and no square corners. It's still a quadrilateral.
So a square is a rectangle and a rhombus?
Yes! Four square corners make it a rectangle. Four equal sides make it a rhombus.
Our play area is a rectangle. Now let's measure it two ways.
Area is how many unit squares cover a shape.
area
Here is one unit square. Each side is one metre long.
It covers one square metre. We write that as one sq m.
1 square metre = 1 sq m
Let's lay squares row by row. Count with me!
Five, ten, fifteen, twenty.
Twenty squares cover it. The area is twenty square metres.
area = 20 sq m
Counting takes a while. Is there a faster way?
It has four rows, and five squares in each row.
4 rows of 5
Rows times columns: four times five is twenty square metres.
So my eighteen mats were two short. Twenty squares need twenty mats!
Fun fact: bees build honeycomb from six-sided cells. They fit with no gaps, like floor tiles.
Perimeter is the distance all the way around the edge.
perimeter
Watch the glowing dot walk the edge, one metre at a time.
Add the sides: four plus five plus four plus five is eighteen metres.
Eighteen metres of edge. That's why eighteen fence pieces fit!
Perimeter is a length, so we measure it in metres.
Area counts squares, so we measure it in square metres.
perimeter: m    area: sq m
The fence goes around. The mats cover inside. Two different jobs!
Fun fact: perimeter comes from two Greek words, peri, around, and metron, measure.
peri = around, metron = measure
My turn! Here's a three by three square. I'll find its perimeter.
I'll count the squares along the edge.
Eight squares, so the perimeter is eight metres!
Hmm. How many edge units are there really? Think!
Walk the edge, not the squares.
Three on each side, twelve in all. The perimeter is twelve metres.
Look at a corner square. It touches two edges, so it has two edge units.
I counted each corner once. Count the edges, not the squares!
Walk around the edge, perimeter!
Cover up the middle, area!
Covering inside?
Area!
Going around?
Perimeter!
One more time, everybody!
Walk around the edge, perimeter!
Cover up the middle, area!
Paint the middle with a flat hand. Walk the edge with two fingers!
Hello! I have exactly twelve fence pieces, and I want the grassiest pen.
Twelve pieces make a perimeter of twelve metres. Let's try three pens.
Which pen will hold the most grass? Think!
Pen A is one by five. One plus five plus one plus five is twelve metres.
One row of five is five square metres.
Pen B is two by four. Two plus four plus two plus four is twelve metres.
Two rows of four is eight square metres.
Pen C is three by three. Three plus three plus three plus three is twelve metres.
Three rows of three is nine square metres!
Same fence, three different areas: five, eight and nine square metres!
The square pen has the most grass. I'll take that one!
Same perimeter doesn't mean same area. Wow!
Real jobs! Does each job need area, covering, or perimeter, going around?
Carpet for a floor?
Area! Carpet covers the floor.
A ribbon round a picture frame?
Perimeter! The ribbon goes around the frame.
Tiles on a bathroom floor?
Area! Tiles cover the floor.
A fence round a garden?
Perimeter! A fence goes around.
Paint for a wall?
Area! Paint covers the wall.
Challenge time! Help us finish the playground. First, the sandbox.
It's three metres by four metres. What is its area?
Three rows of four: twelve square metres.
Now its perimeter. How far around?
Fourteen metres. Square metres for area, metres for perimeter.
Next, an L-shaped splash pad. How can we find its area?
Split it into two rectangles. Two rows of four is eight square metres.
Two rows of two is four. Eight plus four is twelve square metres.
Last one. The rectangle's perimeter is ten metres. One side is three metres.
How long is each missing side?
Three plus three is six. Ten take away six leaves four metres.
Two equal sides share four, so each one is two metres.
Measure twice: count the edge.
Quiz! A rectangle is two squares by six squares. What is its area?
Two times six: twelve square units!
2 × 6 = 12 square units
And its perimeter?
Two plus six plus two plus six is sixteen units!
A ribbon round a card: area or perimeter?
Perimeter! It goes around.
Is a square a rectangle?
Yes! It has four sides and four square corners.
Two pens both have twelve metres of fence. Same area?
Not always! Two by four holds eight square metres. Three by three holds nine.
Area covers: count squares, or rows times columns. Perimeter goes around: add the sides.
Same perimeter, different areas. And a square is a rectangle and a rhombus!
Twenty square metres of grass and eighteen metres of fence. The playground is open!
Measured twice, built once!
Bye, builders!
